name: Reverse X-Guard Entry
description: Learn Reverse X-Guard Entry from inverted guard. Step-by-step execution for leg entanglement access. Success rates: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
Reverse X-Guard Entry is a dynamic transition from inverted guard that establishes powerful leg entanglement control beneath your opponent. Unlike standard X-Guard where you face your opponent, Reverse X-Guard positions you facing away, with your hooks controlling their near leg while your body extends beneath them. This creates exceptional off-balancing potential and sweep opportunities that are difficult to defend because your opponent cannot see your lower body mechanics.

The entry requires precise timing and hip mobility, as you must thread your legs through while maintaining upper body connection. The position excels against opponents who maintain upright posture from inverted guard rather than applying stack pressure. Once established, Reverse X-Guard offers high-percentage sweeps, transitions to standard X-Guard, Single Leg X entries, and direct back take opportunities when opponents overcommit to regaining base.

This technique represents a sophisticated evolution in modern guard play, bridging inverted guard mobility with the powerful mechanical advantages of X-Guard systems. Practitioners who develop proficiency find it becomes a reliable pathway when standard berimbolo or back take entries are blocked.
key_principles: Maintain constant hip elevation throughout the entry to prevent being flattened before completing the hook insertion
Control opponent's near-side ankle or pants cuff throughout the transition to prevent them from stepping away and disengaging
Thread your outside leg deep beneath opponent's hips before attempting to establish the crossing hook
Keep your shoulder blades connected to the mat as anchor points while your hips rotate into position
Use opponent's weight distribution against them by timing the entry when they shift weight forward
Establish the crossing hook on their far hip before releasing any upper body grips to ensure position security
setup_requirements: Inverted guard established with shoulders and upper back anchored to the mat, hips elevated
Control of opponent's near-side pants leg at the ankle or cuff to prevent disengagement
Opponent maintaining relatively upright posture rather than applying heavy stack pressure
Clear pathway beneath opponent's hips without their knee blocking the threading angle
Secondary grip on sleeve, collar, or belt to control their upper body during the transition

execution_steps.description: From inverted guard, secure a strong grip on opponent's near-side pants at the ankle or cuff with your same-side hand. Establish a secondary grip on their sleeve or collar with your other hand to prevent them from posting or disengaging.
execution_steps.timing: When opponent is upright with weight neutral

execution_steps.description: Hip escape slightly toward your pants-grip side to create an angle that allows your outside leg to thread beneath their hips. Your shoulder blades remain anchored while your hips rotate approximately 45 degrees.

Shoot your outside leg (the leg furthest from the pants grip) deep beneath opponent's hips, threading between their legs. Your shin should travel past their far hip, positioning your foot to hook behind their far thigh.
execution_steps.timing: As you complete the hip escape motion

execution_steps.description: Curl your threading leg to establish a strong hook behind opponent's far hip or thigh. This crossing hook is the primary control point that prevents them from stepping over or disengaging. Lock your ankle behind their hip crease.
execution_steps.timing: Before releasing any upper body grips

execution_steps.description: With the crossing hook secured, bring your near-side leg up and hook it behind opponent's near-side knee or thigh. This creates the characteristic X configuration with your legs controlling their base from opposite sides.

Release upper body grips and transition your hands to control opponent's far ankle and near knee. Extend your hips to elevate them and complete the Reverse X-Guard position with full mechanical control.

common_counters.counter: Opponent steps far leg back before crossing hook establishes, creating distance and preventing leg threading
common_counters.your_response: Maintain pants grip and follow their retreating leg, using the grip to prevent full disengagement while transitioning to Single Leg X or technical standup

common_counters.counter: Opponent applies immediate stack pressure when they recognize the inversion, driving weight onto your shoulders
common_counters.your_response: Abandon the entry and granby roll to the opposite side, using their forward pressure to assist your rotation and recover to seated guard or De La Riva

common_counters.counter: Opponent posts their hand on your hip to prevent threading and maintains low base
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to attack their posting arm with a two-on-one grip, clearing the obstruction and creating the window for leg insertion

common_counters.counter: Opponent backsteps their near leg to avoid the hook and circles to pass
common_counters.your_response: Follow their backstep motion and convert to Single Leg X on their retreating leg, or use the rotation to enter standard X-Guard

common_errors.error: Attempting entry when opponent is applying heavy stack pressure
common_errors.consequence: Weight compresses your neck and shoulders, eliminating hip mobility needed for threading and creating injury risk
common_errors.correction: Only attempt Reverse X-Guard Entry when opponent is upright; use granby roll escape against stack pressure instead

common_errors.error: Releasing pants grip before establishing the crossing hook
common_errors.consequence: Opponent simply steps away and disengages, leaving you in a compromised inverted position without control
common_errors.correction: Maintain pants grip throughout the entire entry sequence until crossing hook is fully locked behind their hip

common_errors.error: Threading leg too shallow, with hook ending on opponent's near hip instead of far hip
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient control and leverage; opponent easily clears your hook and passes or establishes top control
common_errors.correction: Ensure your threading leg travels completely past their centerline before curling to establish the crossing hook on their far hip

common_errors.error: Allowing shoulders to rise off the mat during hip rotation
common_errors.consequence: Loss of anchor points destabilizes the entry and allows opponent to flatten you or drive you sideways
common_errors.correction: Keep shoulder blades pressed into the mat throughout; only your hips should rotate while shoulders remain fixed

common_errors.error: Rushing to extend hips before both hooks are properly set
common_errors.consequence: Hooks slip out under extension pressure, losing the position and leaving you exposed beneath opponent
common_errors.correction: Verify both the crossing hook and inside hook are locked before any hip extension; position security precedes power generation

training_progressions.description: Practice inverted hip rotation and leg threading movements without a partner. Focus on maintaining shoulder contact while rotating hips 45 degrees, then threading and curling each leg individually. Develop the hip mobility required for clean entries.

Partner holds static upright position from inverted guard while you practice the complete entry sequence. Focus on grip establishment, threading angle, and hook placement. Partner provides feedback on hook depth and position security.

Partner moves naturally from inverted guard top position while you identify windows for entry. Practice recognizing when opponent's posture creates the opening versus when they're applying pressure that requires defensive response.

Full positional sparring from inverted guard with all options available. Chain Reverse X-Guard Entry with berimbolo attempts, back takes, and other X-Guard entries. Partner defends realistically while you develop pattern recognition for optimal entry timing.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Without gi grips available, control opponent's ankle with a c-grip on the Achilles tendon and use an overhook or underhook on their far leg during threading. The entry mechanics remain similar but require more precise timing since grip security is reduced.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: All no-gi situations; when opponent's gi is sweat-soaked and grips are unreliable

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Direct Entry from De La Riva
variants_and_adaptations.description: Rather than establishing inverted guard first, enter Reverse X-Guard directly from De La Riva Guard by inverting while maintaining the DLR hook and immediately threading beneath opponent. This bypasses the intermediate inverted guard position.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent attempts to disengage from De La Riva by stepping back; when you have strong DLR hook and they're off-balance

variants_and_adaptations.description: Initiate as if entering Reverse X-Guard but continue the spin to take the back via Kiss of the Dragon when opponent defends by posting their hand or stepping their far leg back. The entry motion is identical initially.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent reacts strongly to prevent Reverse X-Guard hooks; when back take opportunity appears during entry attempt

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Reverse X-Guard Entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to establish Reverse X-Guard position, where your legs create an X-configuration controlling opponent's base while you face away from them. This position offers powerful sweep mechanics, transitions to other leg entanglements, and back take opportunities that are difficult to defend because opponents cannot see your lower body movements.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Reverse X-Guard Entry from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Inverted Guard with your shoulders and upper back anchored to the mat, hips elevated, and legs positioned toward your opponent. You need an established inverted guard with proper weight distribution and active grips before attempting the entry.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key grips needed for Reverse X-Guard Entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The essential grips are a pants grip on opponent's near-side ankle or cuff with your same-side hand to prevent disengagement, and a secondary grip on their sleeve, collar, or belt with your other hand to control their upper body. The pants grip must be maintained throughout the entire entry until the crossing hook is locked.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the best time to attempt Reverse X-Guard Entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when opponent maintains upright posture from inverted guard top position rather than applying stack pressure. Look for moments when their weight is neutral or slightly forward, creating space beneath their hips for threading. Avoid attempting this when they're driving weight onto your shoulders.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent recognizes your entry and posts their hand on your hip to block threading. How do you respond?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Attack their posting hand with a two-on-one grip using both hands to strip and redirect the obstruction, creating the window for your leg to thread beneath their hips. Alternatively, use the posting hand as a pivot point - their commitment to blocking one pathway often opens another, such as a berimbolo entry on the opposite side.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the critical difference between where the crossing hook must land versus where it commonly ends up as an error?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The crossing hook must travel completely past opponent's centerline to land on their far hip or behind their far thigh. The common error is threading too shallow and hooking the near hip instead. The far hip placement creates true mechanical control and prevents easy clearing, while the near hip placement provides minimal leverage and is easily defeated.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent begins applying stack pressure as you start threading your leg. What immediate adjustment do you make?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Abandon the Reverse X-Guard Entry attempt and execute a granby roll to the opposite side of their pressure. Use their forward driving momentum to assist your rotation rather than fighting against the stack. This converts their offensive pressure into your escape mechanism and allows you to recover to De La Riva, seated guard, or attempt a berimbolo on the other side.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the direction of force differ between Reverse X-Guard sweeps and standard X-Guard sweeps?
knowledge_assessment.answer: In standard X-Guard, you typically sweep by extending your legs and pushing opponent backward or lifting them overhead. In Reverse X-Guard, because you face away from them, your sweeps work by pulling their base out from under them - extending creates a downward pressure on their near leg while your hooks disrupt their far-side base, toppling them sideways or forward over your body rather than backward.

knowledge_assessment.question: What chain attacks should you prepare if opponent successfully defends your Reverse X-Guard Entry by stepping their far leg back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When opponent steps their far leg back, immediately redirect to Single Leg X-Guard on their near leg that remains in range, or use the momentum of their retreat to come up to a technical standup. If you maintain the pants grip during their backstep, you can also follow their motion into a standard X-Guard entry on the retreating leg or convert to a leg drag position as you come up.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must you maintain shoulder blade contact with the mat throughout the entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The shoulder blades serve as fixed anchor points that create rotational stability during the hip movement. If your shoulders rise, you lose the mechanical base needed to generate threading force and become susceptible to being pushed or pulled off-balance. The anchored shoulders also protect your neck from compression and maintain the structural integrity needed for the transition.

safety_considerations: Reverse X-Guard Entry requires significant hip and spine mobility. Practitioners should develop adequate flexibility before attempting this technique in live training. The inverted position places some stress on the cervical spine - always maintain shoulder blade contact with the mat and avoid allowing weight to compress your neck. If opponent applies stack pressure during the entry attempt, immediately abandon and granby roll to prevent neck injury. When drilling, partners should apply graduated resistance and communicate clearly about pressure levels. Practitioners with existing neck or lower back issues should consult with a medical professional and their instructor before incorporating inverted techniques into their game.
position_integration: Reverse X-Guard Entry serves as a critical bridge between inverted guard mobility and the powerful leg entanglement system. It provides an alternative pathway when standard berimbolo or rolling back take attempts are blocked, making your inverted guard game more complete. Once established in Reverse X-Guard, practitioners have access to high-percentage sweeps, transitions to standard X-Guard and Single Leg X-Guard, and direct back take opportunities. This technique integrates particularly well with De La Riva and Reverse De La Riva guard systems, as all three positions share similar gripping strategies and can be chained together fluidly. Developing this entry expands your offensive options from bottom and forces opponents to defend multiple threats simultaneously from your inverted position.
